regimen_profiles.clinical_summary: This treatment is used for eligible high-risk triple-negative breast cancer before surgery, then continued with immunotherapy after surgery when appropriate. Chemotherapy damages cancer cells, while pembrolizumab helps immune cells recognise and attack them. The team considers cancer extent, fitness, heart health and whether immunotherapy is suitable.
regimen_profiles.treatment_setting: Triple-negative breast cancer · neoadjuvant and adjuvant immunotherapy
regimen_profiles.component_rationale: Pembrolizumab: PD-1 is a control switch on T cells, a type of immune cell. When it connects with PD-L1 or PD-L2, the T cell receives a signal to reduce its activity. Some cancers use this pathway to escape immune attack. Pembrolizumab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, helping T cells recognise and attack the cancer. It does not directly poison cancer cells like chemotherapy. Releasing this brake can also allow immune cells to attack healthy organs, which explains the different side-effect pattern and why symptoms can appear after treatment stops. Carboplatin: Carboplatin creates links in DNA, making it harder for cells to copy and repair their genetic instructions. Its dose depends on kidney function as well as the intended regimen. Paclitaxel: Cells use tiny structures called microtubules to separate their chromosomes when dividing. Paclitaxel stabilises these structures so they cannot rearrange normally, interrupting cell division. It can also affect nerves and other healthy tissues. Doxorubicin: Doxorubicin interferes with enzymes and DNA processes needed for cell division. It can also affect heart muscle, so the team considers previous exposure and cardiac risk. Cyclophosphamide: Cyclophosphamide is activated in the body and damages DNA. This helps stop dividing cancer cells but can also affect blood-cell production and reproductive tissues.

regimen_profiles.clinical_summary: This treatment is used for eligible high-risk triple-negative breast cancer before surgery, then continued with immunotherapy after surgery when appropriate. Chemotherapy damages cancer cells, while pembrolizumab helps immune cells recognise and attack them. The team considers cancer extent, fitness, heart health and whether immunotherapy is suitable.
regimen_profiles.treatment_setting: Triple-negative breast cancer · neoadjuvant and adjuvant immunotherapy
regimen_profiles.component_rationale: Pembrolizumab: PD-1 is a control switch on T cells, a type of immune cell. When it connects with PD-L1 or PD-L2, the T cell receives a signal to reduce its activity. Some cancers use this pathway to escape immune attack. Pembrolizumab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, helping T cells recognise and attack the cancer. It does not directly poison cancer cells like chemotherapy. Releasing this brake can also allow immune cells to attack healthy organs, which explains the different side-effect pattern and why symptoms can appear after treatment stops. Carboplatin: Carboplatin creates links in DNA, making it harder for cells to copy and repair their genetic instructions. Its dose depends on kidney function as well as the intended regimen. Paclitaxel: Cells use tiny structures called microtubules to separate their chromosomes when dividing. Paclitaxel stabilises these structures so they cannot rearrange normally, interrupting cell division. It can also affect nerves and other healthy tissues. Doxorubicin: Doxorubicin interferes with enzymes and DNA processes needed for cell division. It can also affect heart muscle, so the team considers previous exposure and cardiac risk. Cyclophosphamide: Cyclophosphamide is activated in the body and damages DNA. This helps stop dividing cancer cells but can also affect blood-cell production and reproductive tissues.
